steps.text: Write $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $F=\widetilde M$. A finite principal cover $D(f_i)$ has sections $M_{f_{i_0}\cdots f_{i_p}}$ on each intersection. The elements $f_i$ generate the unit ideal after suitable powers.

Localize the augmented Čech complex at each $f_i$. The cover then contains the whole local spectrum, so insertion of index $i$ gives a contracting homotopy. These localizations detect zero modules because the $D(f_i)$ cover the spectrum.

Principal covers are cofinal among covers of every affine open, and their intersections are principal opens. The acyclic-basis criterion identifies the zero positive Čech groups with the derived functors $H^q(X,F)$. Thus all positive groups vanish.

source.excerpt: Lemma 30.3.1 . Let $X$ be a scheme. Assume that $X$ is quasi-compact, for every quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$ we have $H^1(X, \mathcal{I}) = 0$. Then $X$ is affine.

steps.text: For a closed point $x$ in an affine open $U$, choose ideals of $X\setminus U$ and $(X\setminus U)\cup\{x\}$. Their quotient is the residue field at $x$. Zero first cohomology lifts its element $1$ to a global function $f$ with $x\in X_f\subset U$.

Each $X_f=D(f|_U)$ is affine. These opens contain all closed points. A nonempty closed complement in the quasi-compact space would have a closed point, so the opens cover $X$. Keep finitely many functions $f_1,\ldots,f_n$.

The map $O_X^n\to O_X$ with entries $f_i$ is surjective on stalks. Its kernel has a finite filtration whose factors are quasi-coherent ideals. Long exact sequences give zero first cohomology of the kernel, so there are global $a_i$ with $\sum a_if_i=1$.

The principal opens $X_{f_i}$ are affine and their functions generate the unit ideal in $A=\Gamma(X,O_X)$. Localization identifies each with $\operatorname{Spec}A_{f_i}$. These identifications agree on intersections and glue to $X\cong\operatorname{Spec}A$.

steps.text: Take an injective resolution $F\to J^\bullet$ and form the double complex of its Čech sections. The augmented Čech complex of each injective sheaf is exact, so one filtration computes $H^*(X,F)$.
The other filtration has terms $\prod H^q(U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_p},F)$. Affine vanishing makes every row with $q>0$ zero. The row with $q=0$ is the Čech complex of $F$.
Both filtrations compute the same total cohomology. Only the section row survives, so its degree-$q$ cohomology equals $H^q(X,F)$. The comparison respects multiplication by global functions.

source.citation: The Stacks Project Authors, The Stacks Project (2026), Lemma 30.4.5, Tag 01XJ, coherent.
source.excerpt: Lemma 30.4.5 . Let $f : X \to S$ be a morphism of schemes. Assume that $f$ is quasi-separated and quasi-compact. For any quasi-coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ the higher direct images $R^ pf_*\mathcal{F}$ are quasi-coherent on $S$. If $S$ is quasi-compact, there exists an integer $n = n(X, S, f)$ such that $R^ pf_*\mathcal{F} = 0$ for all $p \geq n$ and any quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$. In fact, if $S$ is quasi-compact we can find $n = n(X, S, f)$ such that for every morphism of schemes $S' \to S$ we have $R^ p(f')_*\mathcal{F}' = 0$ for $p \geq n$ and any quasi-coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}'$ on $X'$. Here $f' : X' = S' \times _ S X \to S'$ is the base change of $f$.

steps.text: Higher direct images commute with restriction to base opens. Quasi-coherence is local on the base. We can therefore assume $S$ affine and $X$ quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
For an affine open $U\subset X$, the map $U\to S$ is affine. Its degree-zero pushforward is quasi-coherent, and all positive higher direct images vanish by affine vanishing.

For a union $U\cup V$, relative Mayer-Vietoris expresses each higher direct image as an extension of a kernel and a cokernel of the direct images on $U,V,U\cap V$. Quasi-coherent sheaves form an abelian category. The quasi-compact open induction principle completes the proof.

steps.text: The standard affine charts and all intersections are affine. Čech comparison computes the groups. Each Laurent monomial of total degree $d$ defines a separate weight subcomplex preserved by the differential.
When every exponent is nonnegative, the weight complex is the ordinary simplex complex. It contributes one copy of $A$ in degree zero and nothing in higher degrees.

When every exponent of the weight is negative, the monomial occurs only on the intersection of all n+1 charts. The weight contributes one copy of A in degree n. There are no such monomials for d greater than -n-1.

If the negative-index set is nonempty and proper, choose an index outside it. Insertion of that index, with the Čech sign, defines a homotopy $hd+dh=1$. These complexes are acyclic. The direct sum of all weights gives the asserted formula.

source.excerpt: Lemma 30.16.1 . Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $X \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ be a proper morphism. Let $\mathcal{L}$ be an ample invertible sheaf on $X$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module. The graded ring $A = \bigoplus _{d \geq 0} H^0(X, \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d})$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra. There exists an $r \geq 0$ and $d_1, \ldots , d_ r \in \mathbf{Z}$ and a surjection \[ \bigoplus \nolimits _{j = 1, \ldots , r} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d_ j} \longrightarrow \mathcal{F}. \] For any $p$ the cohomology group $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})$ is a finite $R$-module. If $p > 0$, then $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}) = 0$ for all $d$ large enough. For any $k \in \mathbf{Z}$ the graded $A$-module \[ \bigoplus \nolimits _{d \geq k} H^0(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes _{\mathcal{O}_ X} \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}) \] is a finite $A$-module.

The following are equivalent $\mathcal{L}$ is ample on $X$ (this is equivalent to many other things, see Properties, Proposition 28.27.13 and Morphisms, Lemma 29.40.4 ), for every coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module $\mathcal{F}$ there exists an $n_0 \geq 0$ such that $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}) = 0$ for all $n \geq n_0$ and $p > 0$, and for every quasi-coherent sheaf of ideals $\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{O}_ X$, there exists an $n \geq 1$ such that $H^1(X, \mathcal{I} \otimes \mathcal{L}^{\otimes n}) = 0$.

steps.text: If $L$ is ample, Serre vanishing gives the required threshold for each coherent sheaf $F$. This proves the forward implication with all positive degrees at once.

For the reverse implication, apply the assumed vanishing to coherent ideal sheaves. A first-cohomology obstruction to a section lift disappears after a suitable twist. The section argument of Stacks Lemma 30.3.3 produces powers of $L$ whose nonzero loci form affine neighborhoods of every point.

The affine nonzero loci of sections of positive powers of $L$ form a basis for the topology. This is the section criterion for ampleness. The cited proof supplies the ideal-lift argument, rather than an assertion that arbitrary vanishing implies positivity.
Serre vanishing proves the forward direction. The ideal-section criterion proves the reverse direction. Both hold under properness and the Noetherian base, so the asserted equivalence follows.

applications.title: Decide ampleness of twists on the projective line.
applications.inputs: Let $L=O(a)$ on $\mathbf P^1_k$ with integer $a$.
applications.hypotheses: The scheme X is proper over a Noetherian ring, and L is a line bundle on X.

steps.text: If $a>0$, then for each fixed $b$, the twist $O(b)\otimes L^n=O(b+an)$ eventually has zero first cohomology.
If $a=0$, take $F=O(-2)$. Its first cohomology remains $k$ for every n.
If $a<0$, the same F gives $b+an\le-2$ for all n, so the first cohomology never vanishes.

applications.conclusion: The criterion, together with the known ampleness of O(1), gives ampleness exactly when $a>0$.

steps.text: A finite morphism is affine, hence quasi-affine. Pullback along a quasi-affine morphism preserves an ample line bundle. This gives the forward implication.

Assume $f^*L$ ample. For a coherent sheaf G on X, require eventual vanishing of positive cohomology of $G\otimes L^n$. If the two outside sheaves of a short exact sequence have this property, the long exact sequence gives it for the middle sheaf. Thus the property is closed under extensions and finite direct sums, as Lemma 30.12.8 requires.

For each integral closed support Z with generic point xi, Lemmas 30.13.1 and 30.13.2 provide a pushforward G=f_*F supported on Z with maximal-ideal annihilation at xi. If J_xi=O_X,xi, they identify JG with f_*(f^(-1)J F). The projection formula and ample vanishing on Y prove eventual vanishing for every such ideal modification.

The devissage proves eventual vanishing for every coherent sheaf on $X$. The cohomological ampleness criterion therefore makes $L$ ample. Surjectivity is essential to supply a support piece over each component. Coherent devissage in Lemma 30.12.8 gives this implication.
The first step proves that ampleness pulls back. The last three steps prove that an ample pullback forces ampleness on X. These implications give the stated equivalence.

steps.text: Let $I$ define $Z$. Its support condition and Noetherian finiteness give $I^N=0$. The intermediate schemes cut out by the powers of $I$ reduce the converse to a square-zero thickening.

For $I^2=0$, the sequence $0\to I\otimes L^n\to L^n\to i_*i^*L^n\to0$ measures the lift obstruction. On the affine nonzero locus of an ample section $s$ on $Z$, localization kills this obstruction. The lifted section has the same nonzero locus topologically. A nilpotent thickening of an affine scheme is affine. These loci cover $X$ and form the section basis for ampleness. The forward implication follows by restriction of an ample bundle.

Then there exist an $n \geq 0$ and a diagram \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[rd] & X' \ar[d] \ar[l]^\pi \ar[r] & \mathbf{P}^ n_ S \ar[dl] \\ & S & } \] where $X' \to \mathbf{P}^ n_ S$ is an immersion, and $\pi : X' \to X$ is proper and surjective. Moreover, we may arrange it such that there exists a dense open subscheme $U \subset X$ such that $\pi ^{-1}(U) \to U$ is an isomorphism.

steps.text: The published construction chooses finitely many affine opens meeting every generic point. Their intersection U is dense. Replace X by the scheme-theoretic closure of U if needed, which preserves surjectivity and the isomorphism over U.
Embed each affine chart into a projective space over S, then take the closure of the diagonal copy of U in their product. The projections to the chart closures are proper.

The inverse images of the charts form an open subscheme X prime of the closed diagonal closure Z, hence a locally closed subscheme of the projective product. The projections agree on the scheme-theoretically dense U. Separatedness of X makes them agree on overlaps, so they define a morphism to X.

The inclusion V_i into pi^(-1)(U_i) is proper over U_i, so its image is closed. It contains the scheme-theoretically dense common open U, hence pi^(-1)(U_i)=V_i. The same argument gives pi^(-1)(U)=U. Properness is therefore local on the chart cover, and the image is closed and contains dense U. A Segre embedding makes X prime quasi-projective.

Chow modifies an integral closed support Z by a projective Z prime. Choose a line bundle ample for both the modification and the map to the base. A large power has zero positive direct images for both maps. Relative vanishing is Lemma 30.16.2, obtained by ample vanishing on affine base opens.

source.excerpt: Theorem 30.20.5 (Theorem on formal functions) . Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring. Let $I \subset A$ be an ideal. Let $f : X \to \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$ be a proper morphism. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent sheaf on $X$. Fix $p \geq 0$. The system of maps \[ H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})/I^ nH^ p(X, \mathcal{F}) \longrightarrow H^ p(X, \mathcal{F}/I^ n\mathcal{F}) \] define an isomorphism of limits \[ H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})^\wedge \longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{lim}}\nolimits _ n H^ p(X, \mathcal{F}/I^ n\mathcal{F}) \] where the left hand side is the completion of the $A$-module $H^ p(X, \mathcal{F})$ with respect to the ideal $I$, see Algebra, Section 10.96 . Moreover, this is in fact a homeomorphism for the limit topologies.

The Mittag-Leffler stabilization identifies $\varprojlim M_n$ with $\varprojlim N_n$, with their limit topologies. Each $N_n$ is the quotient $M/K_n$.

The sections generate on the chosen fiber. Their failure locus is closed, and its image under the proper map is closed and misses y. Remove that image to obtain a map $\varphi:X\to\mathbf P^r_Y$ with $L^d=\varphi^*O(1)$.

The proper map $\varphi$ has finite fibers above the projective fiber at y. The local finiteness theorem and properness of the projective target over Y permit a further base restriction on which $\varphi$ is finite. Finiteness near the fiber is Lemma 30.21.2.

Pullback of $O(1)$ along the finite map is relatively ample. Thus $L^d$, and hence L, is relatively ample on the resulting neighborhood. The statement gives existence of a neighborhood, not a global conclusion.

source.excerpt: Lemma 30.22.1 . Let $A$ be a Noetherian ring and set $S = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(A)$. Let $f : X \to S$ be a proper morphism of schemes. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a coherent $\mathcal{O}_ X$-module flat over $S$. Then $R\Gamma (X, \mathcal{F})$ is a perfect object of $D(A)$, and for any ring map $A \to A'$ the base change map \[ R\Gamma (X, \mathcal{F}) \otimes _ A^{\mathbf{L}} A' \longrightarrow R\Gamma (X_{A'}, \mathcal{F}_{A'}) \] is an isomorphism.

steps.text: Take a finite affine cover of the separated source. Its alternating Čech complex K computes derived global sections and is bounded. Relative flatness of F makes its terms flat A-modules.
Affine localization and tensor identify $K\otimes_A B$ with the Čech complex of $F_B$ on $X_B$. Since K is a bounded flat complex, ordinary tensor equals derived tensor.

Proper coherence gives finite A-modules $H^q(K)$. To bound Tor amplitude against any A-module M, use the square-zero algebra $A\oplus M$. The same base-change model has a uniform bounded range of cohomology. Thus K is pseudo-coherent with finite Tor amplitude, and is perfect. The derived-algebra criteria are More on Algebra Lemmas 15.66.17 and 15.76.2.

The bounded flat model gives the comparison for every A-algebra B. Its finite cohomology and finite Tor amplitude make it perfect. These are the two asserted conclusions for the same derived global-sections object.

steps.text: The universally closed factorization lemma constructs $S′=\operatorname{Spec}_S(f_*O_X)$ and the natural map g. It proves that $\pi$ is integral and that $g_*O_X=O_{S′}$. The inherited finite-type and separated properties make g proper.

Work on an affine S prime. Flat base change preserves the identity of global functions under affine étale extensions. To prove geometric connectedness it suffices to prove connectedness of fibers after all such pointed étale extensions.

The proper idempotent-lift lemma lifts an idempotent of a fiber to the base after localization. Its image factors through the residue field, whose only idempotents are 0 and 1. A nonempty fiber with no nontrivial idempotent is connected. This proves geometric connectedness after the tests. The idempotent-lift input is Derived Categories of Schemes Lemma 36.32.7.

steps.text: The sheaf $\mu_n$ consists by definition of units u with $u^n=1$. Its inclusion is injective and its image is exactly the kernel of the nth-power map.
For a unit a on an affine test scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$, form $B=A[T]/(T^n-a)$. It is finite free of rank n, hence faithfully flat. The root T is a unit in B because its nth power is a unit.

The derivative $nT^{n-1}$ is a unit in B. Thus $A\to B$ is standard étale and Spec B is a surjective étale cover. On this cover a is the nth power of T. These covers prove sheaf surjectivity on each étale site, including n equal to 1.

The kernel is mu_n by the first step. Every unit acquires an nth root on the surjective etale cover of the third step. Thus the power map has exactly this kernel and is locally surjective, which proves exactness.

source.excerpt: Proposition 59.45.4 (Topological invariance of étale cohomology) . Let $X_0 \to X$ be a universal homeomorphism of schemes (for example the closed immersion defined by a nilpotent sheaf of ideals). Then the étale sites $X_{\acute{e}tale}$ and $(X_0)_{\acute{e}tale}$ are isomorphic, the étale topoi $\mathop{\mathit{Sh}}\nolimits (X_{\acute{e}tale})$ and $\mathop{\mathit{Sh}}\nolimits ((X_0)_{\acute{e}tale})$ are equivalent, and $H^ q_{\acute{e}tale}(X, \mathcal{F}) = H^ q_{\acute{e}tale}(X_0, \mathcal{F}|_{X_0})$ for all $q$ and for any abelian sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X_{\acute{e}tale}$.

steps.text: The published topological-invariance theorem shows that base change gives an equivalence between the categories of étale schemes over X and over $X_0$. This uses the integral, radicial, and surjective properties of u, rather than a homeomorphism of ordinary spaces alone. The object equivalence is Theorem 59.45.2.

Surjectivity of a family after base change is equivalent to surjectivity before base change because u is a universal homeomorphism. The category equivalence therefore preserves the étale topology and induces an equivalence of sheaf categories.

Under this equivalence, global sections agree and abelian injectives correspond. Apply the equivalence to an injective resolution of F. The cohomology of the section complexes is identical in every degree.

source.excerpt: Lemma 59.55.1 . Let $R$ be a strictly henselian local ring. Set $S = \mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}(R)$ and let $\overline{s}$ be its closed point. Then the global sections functor $\Gamma (S, -) : \textit{Ab}(S_{\acute{e}tale}) \to \textit{Ab}$ is exact. In fact we have $\Gamma (S, \mathcal{F}) = \mathcal{F}_{\overline{s}}$ for any sheaf of sets $\mathcal{F}$. In particular \[ \forall p\geq 1, \quad H_{\acute{e}tale}^ p(S, \mathcal{F})=0 \] for all $\mathcal{F}\in \textit{Ab}(S_{\acute{e}tale})$.

steps.text: Choose an affine neighborhood of the point in an étale S-scheme. The henselian étale splitting theorem gives an R-algebra decomposition $A=R\times A^\prime$ compatible with the geometric closed point. Thus the neighborhood has an S-section through that point.

The identity neighborhood S is cofinal in the pointed neighborhood system because of these sections. The colimit that defines the geometric stalk therefore equals the sections on S. This holds for any sheaf of sets.

For abelian sheaves, geometric stalks are exact functors. The identified section functor is therefore exact. Its positive derived functors vanish, which is exactly the stated étale-cohomology vanishing.

steps.text: The map $F-1:O_X\to O_X$ sends t to $t^p-t$. Its kernel is the constant sheaf $\mathbf F_p$. For any local section a, the monic polynomial $T^p-T-a$ defines a finite free cover with derivative -1, so the map is surjective as an étale sheaf map.

Etale and Zariski cohomology agree for quasi-coherent modules. Since X is affine, the affine vanishing theorem gives $H^r_{et}(X,O_X)=0$ for every $r>0$. The quasi-coherent comparison is Theorem 59.22.4.

For $q\ge2$, the exact sequence places $H^q_{et}(X,\mathbf F_p)$ between the zero groups $H^{q-1}(X,O_X)$ and $H^q(X,O_X)$. It is therefore zero. Degree one need not vanish because the section map $F-1$ need not be surjective.

steps.text: For the generic inclusion j and the closed point inclusions $i_x$, smoothness gives $0\to\mathbf G_m\to j_*\mathbf G_{m,\eta}\to\bigoplus_x i_{x*}\mathbf Z\to0$. The valuation map is locally surjective because divisors on a regular curve are locally principal.

For each component, Lemma 59.67.12 (Tag 03RG) gives zero positive multiplicative cohomology for its function field and algebraic extensions, using Tsen. Lemma 59.68.2 (Tag 03RJ) computes the stalks and proves R^q j_*G_m=0. Lemma 59.68.3 (Tag 03RK) then uses Leray to prove acyclicity of generic units. Use the disjoint union of generic points for a disconnected smooth curve.

Each closed point has algebraically closed residue field, so its positive cohomology is zero. Finite direct image is exact. Filtered-colimit compatibility therefore gives zero positive cohomology of the direct sum of point sheaves. This is Lemma 59.68.4 (Tag 03RL).
The exact sequence now places $H^q(X,\mathbf G_m)$ between zero groups for $q\ge2$. It therefore vanishes. The degree-one group is the Picard group, which need not be zero.

steps.text: Etale localization expresses a smooth morphism through affine-space charts. Composition reduces it to relative dimension one. Express F as the filtered colimit of its n-torsion parts, with n invertible on S. Higher direct images commute with these colimits. The colimit input is Lemma 59.51.7.

Relative Mayer-Vietoris reduces T to affine pieces. Induction on q and an injective resolution reduce the task to zero higher direct images of a pulled-back injective n-torsion sheaf. Limit descent reduces the affine bases to finite type over $\mathbf Z[1/n]$. Noetherian limit descent uses Lemmas 59.51.8 and 59.51.9.

First reduce to smooth relative curves with geometrically connected fibers and a section. Lemma 59.89.1 kills a generic class after finite field extensions by an etale Galois cover split over that section, with order dividing a power of n. Fundamental Groups Lemma 58.31.8 extends that cover after finite normalization of the bases. Lemma 59.51.5 spreads generic vanishing to a nonempty open V of T.

Injectivity gives a split embedding into j_*I|_V plus i_*I_prime for the closed complement Z. Induction in degrees below q gives the Leray injection from H^q(Y,j_prime_*e_V^(-1)I|_V) into H^q(Y_V,e_V^(-1)I|_V), so the open contribution is zero. The closed contribution dies locally by induction on dim Z, which is less than dim T. This kills the class and completes the comparison.

Lemma 59.87.2 proves the degree-zero comparison for smooth base change. Thus the map $f^{-1}g_*F\to h_*e^{-1}F$ is an isomorphism. This gives the initial case needed by induction on q and, in particular, the preceding-degree comparison when q equals 1.

steps.text: A finite map from X to affine d-space exists for $d=\dim X$. Finite etale direct image has no positive derived functors, so Leray reduces the bound to arbitrary torsion sheaves on affine d-space. Dimension zero is the finite-map case. The finite-map vanishing is Proposition 59.55.2. If cd(K) is infinite, the inequality is automatic.

Embed affine d-space in P^1 times affine (d-1)-space. Lemma 59.95.5 embeds a field of cohomological dimension 1 into each relevant strict-local punctured algebra. That algebra is a filtered limit of lower-dimensional algebras over the field, so induction and Lemmas 59.95.2 and 59.95.4 bound R^q j_* supports by residue transcendence degree d-q. Lemma 59.74.5 and Theorem 59.51.3 convert the support decomposition to boundary cohomology bounds.

The projective-line projection has higher direct images only through degree two. The boundary projection is an isomorphism. Thus for $q>2$, the relative affine-line direct image has the boundary support bound. For q equal to 2, the generic stalk is zero by the curve case. Lemma 59.92.2 gives the proper relative-dimension-one bound, and Theorem 59.53.1 identifies the generic stalk with affine-curve cohomology.

For q equal to 0 or 1, the induction on affine $(d-1)$-space gives the required bound. The sharper boundary estimate treats q at least 2. Every term with total degree greater than $d+\operatorname{cd}K$ vanishes, so the final Leray sequence proves the claim.

Lemma 59.95.3 proves the cohomological dimension bound for affine curves. Together with the dimension-zero finite-map argument, it starts the induction on dimension. The affine-curve vanishing also supplies the degree-two generic-fiber vanishing in the relative Leray argument.

computations.why: Affine space of relative dimension one is smooth over any base. In Z[1/ell] the integer ell is a unit. Thus both the smoothness condition and the invertibility condition hold.

The constant étale sheaf Z/ell has stalks annihilated by ell; every element order divides this invertible integer. The fiber product A^1_S times_S T is A^1_T. These choices satisfy the torsion and cartesian-square conditions.

Inverse image takes the constant sheaf Z/ell on T to the constant sheaf Z/ell on A^1_T. Since g is quasi-compact and quasi-separated the theorem applies and gives f^(-1)R^q g_*F isomorphic to R^q h_*Z/ell on A^1_S for every q>=0.
A^2_k is the spectrum of k[x1,x2]; this algebra is finitely generated over k and has Krull dimension two. Thus the affine and finite-type hypotheses hold.
An algebraically closed field has trivial absolute Galois group. Its étale global-sections functor on abelian sheaves is exact; hence its torsion étale cohomological dimension is zero.

The bound gives cd(A^2_k)<=2+0=2. By the torsion-sheaf definition of cohomological dimension this means H^q_et(A^2_k,F)=0 for every torsion abelian sheaf F and every q>2. No constant-sheaf restriction is required.
